{"type":"tool_call_update","toolCallId":"call-81b7d840-fa31-4798-9b76-f824b66813c3-2","status":"in_progress","content":[{"type":"content","content":{"type":"text","text":" same shelf sized for the wide bin: three columns instead of two.\"\n\n[variants.shelf_gridfinity_3x2.params]\ngrid_x = 3\nbracket_count = 6\n\n[variants.shelf_gridfinity_3x2.accepted]\nsliver = 26\n```\n\nThe test is whether it is the same geometry. A wider cradle on the same J is a variant.\nA different mechanism is a part, however similar the slab looks.\n\n`note` is one sentence saying why the variant exists, written in the user's words rather than the doctrine's, because the viewer shows it next to the variant and its reader is whoever is about to print the thing. The params are the how and never the why: `diagonal = true` explains nothing to someone who has not read the doctrine, and \"prints tilted so it needs no supports\" does.\n\n## Measurements\n\nThe bottleneck on a one-off is not geometry, it is dimensions. A wrong number produces a\nperfect model of the wrong object, and nothing downstream can catch it.\n\n**Ask for a measurement. Never improvise one.** A guessed clearance that happens to\nbuild is worse than a failure, because it prints. Record what you are told in\n`measurements.toml` at the project root, with how it was obtained, and read it with\n`measured()`:\n\n```toml\n[shelf_depth]\nvalue = 340\nunit = \"mm\"\nhow = \"tape measure, freezer middle shelf, 2026-07-20\"\n```\n\n```python\nfrom nurb import measured\n\ndepth = measured(\"shelf_depth\")\n```\n\nAn unknown name raises, naming what is on file. That failure is the point: it is the\nmoment to ask rather than to pick something plausible.\n\n**A published number is a measurement, not a guess.** When the part mates with a manufactured product or a published standard, a VESA mount, a gridfinity bin, a camera thread, the number already exists in a datasheet, and making somebody caliper a hole pattern a standards body fixed is friction wearing rigor's clothes. Research it, record it like any other measurement with `how` naming the source (\"VESA MIS-D 100, manufacturer product page\"), and ask only for what nobody published, like the opening the finished thing has to fit. Two limits keep this honest: the user's actual object outranks the spec when the two disagree, because clones drift, and a number inferred from a product photo or a listing's marketing copy was never published at all, so it is a guess and gets marked like one.\n\n**A photo is a shape, never a dimension.** It can identify the standard, that the siding is dutch lap, that the rail is 2020 extrusion, and the published profile carries the numbers from there. Pixels carry no millimetres, so a dimension read off a photo is a guess and gets marked like one.\n\n**A phone scan is reference geometry, not metrology.** Its error changes with the phone, capture mode, surface and technique, so no universal millimetre threshold makes it a caliper. `nurb scan` reads the mesh in mm, states the units it used, and slices profile polylines to sketch against. Record what it gave with `how` naming the file and the slice, and keep every scan-derived fit `provisional` until a coupon proves it against the real object.\n\n**A fit coupon turns a loose measurement into a tight one.** Before printing a part modelled against a scan or a photo, print the mating surface alone: a thin strip carrying just the profile, minutes of filament. Held against the real object it shows every gap the numbers hid, the parameters get corrected, and only then does the full part print. A coupon that fits is what takes the provisional flag off.\n\n**When there is nobody to ask**, write the guess down and mark it `provisional = true`.\nThe danger was never the guess, it is that a guess and a measurement look identical six\nmonths later. `how` is still required, because \"eyeballed against a broom\" tells the\nnext person how far to trust it, and `nurb check` lists every provisional value until\nsomebody picks up a caliper.\n\nA measured value pays for itself across a family. Notch measured one bracket pitch and\namortized it over sixteen parts.\n\n## Assemblies\n\nEvery rule above judges one solid being manufactured. An assembly judges solids being\nused together: a door on its mount, a lid over the machine it covers. The failure it\nexists for built clean, checked clean, exported watertight and printed beautifully,\nthen jammed at 45 degrees of its swing, because the collision between two correct\nparts existed only in the physical world. No per-solid rule can have an opinion about\nmotion.\n\nThe contract mirrors a part's. An assembly is a function in `parts/` whose keyword\ndefaults are its parameters; what it returns is placed solids rather than one solid.\n`use(name)` builds a sibling part where it was modelled, `hinge(solid, axis, through,\nat)` declares a revolute joint and poses it, and `obstacle(solid, name)` adds what the\nparts mount into: the machine, the wall, the shelf above. The joint angle is an\nordinary keyword default, so the viewer's slider swings it live, and the slider ends\nexactly where the declared range does.\n\n**The declared range is a claim, and `nurb check` audits it** the way min_wall audits\na wall: each hinge sweeps through it against everything else in the scene, and a\nfinding is the angle where it jams plus the coordinates of the contact. Declare what\nthe design needs, never what happens to pass. A door that must stay open by gravity\nneeds past 90 degrees; declaring (0, 90) because that sweeps clean is writing the test\nto match the bug.\n\n**Nothing full width may cross the pivot line.** The mount that carries a hinge has to\nreach the pin from somewhere, so some of it always lives above or behind the pin, and\nany full-width material on the moving part that reaches past the pivot sweeps straight\ninto it. The door that jammed at 45 did so against its own top edge, carried past the\npin to support the knuckles; the knuckles got narrow tabs instead, sized to pass\nbeside the mount, and the panel now starts at the pivot line.\n\n**Obstacles are boxes and prisms, never thin hand-drawn profiles.** Three nearly\ncollinear points make a razor sliver, and OCCT answers a boolean against a degenerate\nsolid with chunks of the other operand: measured once as a 152,000mm3 phantom\ncollision at a pose that was actually clear. The sweep refuses any intersection that\nis not a subset of its inputs and names the solid to fix, but the fix is to model the\nobstacle as something with honest volume in the first place.\n\n**Tangent is clear, and clear is not clearance.** Collision is intersection volume, so\ntwo faces that kiss at zero volume pass, the closed door resting on its stop included.\nIn plastic a zero-clearance pass is already a bind. The declared range should carry\nthe same honesty about clearance that a tongue's `fit` carries about width. The fits\ntable puts numbers to that honesty: 0.3mm is the least a moving pair carries through\nits whole travel, and 0.5mm is what never binds.\n\n**The stop the sweep finds can be the detent the design wants.** The door that\nmotivated all of this rests open at 240 degrees against the back of its own mount,\nheld there by gravity, and that contact is a feature with a card entry, not a finding\nto engineer away. Read a jam before redesigning around it.\n\n**Never trust a swing worked out by hand.** The same hinge was hand-modelled three times and gave three answers, one of them \"impossible\"; the wrong one ran a convex test against a non-convex profile, which is exactly the kind of quiet modelling error a kernel boolean cannot make. The sweep is the authority.\n\n**The sweep is priced per pose, and the declaration sets the pose count.** Every step is a kernel boolean against the rest of the scene, so a door walking 90 degrees at the default 3-degree step is cheap, while a full-circle rotor at the same step is 120 poses and can hold the check for seconds on real geometry. A clean sweep pays the whole walk, since only a jam stops it early. `through=(0, 360)` at the default step is a fine-grained jam audit, not a formality: a free spinner that only needs a gross clearance check should declare a larger `step`, and a range wider than the design actually claims buys nothing but poses.\n\nOne hinge sweeps at a time; the others hold their pose, which is the conservative\nreading of a mechanism you can only move one hand at a time. Printability rules stay\noff assemblies entirely: each part already answered them alone, and overhang measured\non an assembled scene reports confident nonsense.\n\n## Verification\n\n\"It built\" is not verification. `nurb verify` runs the machine-checkable part of\nthis list: one solid per configuration, every count flexed upward, the rules clean,\nand the card agreeing with the geometry. `--report` writes the verdict into\n`build/renders/<part>.verify.md` with the renders that back it beside it, one still\nper finding. The two it cannot do are the two that need you, and they are items 2 and 6.\n\nBefore presenting a part:\n\n1. **Flex the driving parameters up as well as down**, for example 4 to 6 to 2 to 4.\n   Growth is what catches a frozen selector; shrinking alone passes a broken part.\n2. **Check fit-critical faces by coordinate** after any polish or resize. `nurb inspect`\n   lists them, with each finding resolved to the face it fired on. Which faces are\n   fit-critical is still yours to know, which is why this is not something `nurb verify`\n   can run for you.\n3. **Confirm the solid count**, which is almost always one.\n4. **Run `nurb check`.** Zero findings is the bar, and a finding fired at a part that\n   prints fine is a bug in the rule, not something to accept quietly.\n5. **Predict a baseline before you look at it.** Working out what the sliver count\n   should be from the polish exclusions turns the number into a test of the rule instead\n   of something to write down.\n6. **Render it and actually look.** `nurb render <part>` writes a PNG, `--section\n   z:4mm` cuts it open where outside views cannot reach, and `nurb inspect --render`\n   stands a camera at every finding with the guilty face painted. A part can pass\n   every numeric check and still be visibly wrong.\n\n"}}],"rawOutput":{"type":"Bash","output":[],"output_for_prompt":" same shelf sized for the wide bin: three columns instead of two.\"\n\n[variants.shelf_gridfinity_3x2.params]\ngrid_x = 3\nbracket_count = 6\n\n[variants.shelf_gridfinity_3x2.accepted]\nsliver = 26\n```\n\nThe test is whether it is the same geometry. A wider cradle on the same J is a variant.\nA different mechanism is a part, however similar the slab looks.\n\n`note` is one sentence saying why the variant exists, written in the user's words rather than the doctrine's, because the viewer shows it next to the variant and its reader is whoever is about to print the thing. The params are the how and never the why: `diagonal = true` explains nothing to someone who has not read the doctrine, and \"prints tilted so it needs no supports\" does.\n\n## Measurements\n\nThe bottleneck on a one-off is not geometry, it is dimensions. A wrong number produces a\nperfect model of the wrong object, and nothing downstream can catch it.\n\n**Ask for a measurement. Never improvise one.** A guessed clearance that happens to\nbuild is worse than a failure, because it prints. Record what you are told in\n`measurements.toml` at the project root, with how it was obtained, and read it with\n`measured()`:\n\n```toml\n[shelf_depth]\nvalue = 340\nunit = \"mm\"\nhow = \"tape measure, freezer middle shelf, 2026-07-20\"\n```\n\n```python\nfrom nurb import measured\n\ndepth = measured(\"shelf_depth\")\n```\n\nAn unknown name raises, naming what is on file. That failure is the point: it is the\nmoment to ask rather than to pick something plausible.\n\n**A published number is a measurement, not a guess.** When the part mates with a manufactured product or a published standard, a VESA mount, a gridfinity bin, a camera thread, the number already exists in a datasheet, and making somebody caliper a hole pattern a standards body fixed is friction wearing rigor's clothes. Research it, record it like any other measurement with `how` naming the source (\"VESA MIS-D 100, manufacturer product page\"), and ask only for what nobody published, like the opening the finished thing has to fit. Two limits keep this honest: the user's actual object outranks the spec when the two disagree, because clones drift, and a number inferred from a product photo or a listing's marketing copy was never published at all, so it is a guess and gets marked like one.\n\n**A photo is a shape, never a dimension.** It can identify the standard, that the siding is dutch lap, that the rail is 2020 extrusion, and the published profile carries the numbers from there. Pixels carry no millimetres, so a dimension read off a photo is a guess and gets marked like one.\n\n**A phone scan is reference geometry, not metrology.** Its error changes with the phone, capture mode, surface and technique, so no universal millimetre threshold makes it a caliper. `nurb scan` reads the mesh in mm, states the units it used, and slices profile polylines to sketch against. Record what it gave with `how` naming the file and the slice, and keep every scan-derived fit `provisional` until a coupon proves it against the real object.\n\n**A fit coupon turns a loose measurement into a tight one.** Before printing a part modelled against a scan or a photo, print the mating surface alone: a thin strip carrying just the profile, minutes of filament. Held against the real object it shows every gap the numbers hid, the parameters get corrected, and only then does the full part print. A coupon that fits is what takes the provisional flag off.\n\n**When there is nobody to ask**, write the guess down and mark it `provisional = true`.\nThe danger was never the guess, it is that a guess and a measurement look identical six\nmonths later. `how` is still required, because \"eyeballed against a broom\" tells the\nnext person how far to trust it, and `nurb check` lists every provisional value until\nsomebody picks up a caliper.\n\nA measured value pays for itself across a family. Notch measured one bracket pitch and\namortized it over sixteen parts.\n\n## Assemblies\n\nEvery rule above judges one solid being manufactured. An assembly judges solids being\nused together: a door on its mount, a lid over the machine it covers. The failure it\nexists for built clean, checked clean, exported watertight and printed beautifully,\nthen jammed at 45 degrees of its swing, because the collision between two correct\nparts existed only in the physical world. No per-solid rule can have an opinion about\nmotion.\n\nThe contract mirrors a part's. An assembly is a function in `parts/` whose keyword\ndefaults are its parameters; what it returns is placed solids rather than one solid.\n`use(name)` builds a sibling part where it was modelled, `hinge(solid, axis, through,\nat)` declares a revolute joint and poses it, and `obstacle(solid, name)` adds what the\nparts mount into: the machine, the wall, the shelf above. The joint angle is an\nordinary keyword default, so the viewer's slider swings it live, and the slider ends\nexactly where the declared range does.\n\n**The declared range is a claim, and `nurb check` audits it** the way min_wall audits\na wall: each hinge sweeps through it against everything else in the scene, and a\nfinding is the angle where it jams plus the coordinates of the contact. Declare what\nthe design needs, never what happens to pass. A door that must stay open by gravity\nneeds past 90 degrees; declaring (0, 90) because that sweeps clean is writing the test\nto match the bug.\n\n**Nothing full width may cross the pivot line.** The mount that carries a hinge has to\nreach the pin from somewhere, so some of it always lives above or behind the pin, and\nany full-width material on the moving part that reaches past the pivot sweeps straight\ninto it. The door that jammed at 45 did so against its own top edge, carried past the\npin to support the knuckles; the knuckles got narrow tabs instead, sized to pass\nbeside the mount, and the panel now starts at the pivot line.\n\n**Obstacles are boxes and prisms, never thin hand-drawn profiles.** Three nearly\ncollinear points make a razor sliver, and OCCT answers a boolean against a degenerate\nsolid with chunks of the other operand: measured once as a 152,000mm3 phantom\ncollision at a pose that was actually clear. The sweep refuses any intersection that\nis not a subset of its inputs and names the solid to fix, but the fix is to model the\nobstacle as something with honest volume in the first place.\n\n**Tangent is clear, and clear is not clearance.** Collision is intersection volume, so\ntwo faces that kiss at zero volume pass, the closed door resting on its stop included.\nIn plastic a zero-clearance pass is already a bind. The declared range should carry\nthe same honesty about clearance that a tongue's `fit` carries about width. The fits\ntable puts numbers to that honesty: 0.3mm is the least a moving pair carries through\nits whole travel, and 0.5mm is what never binds.\n\n**The stop the sweep finds can be the detent the design wants.** The door that\nmotivated all of this rests open at 240 degrees against the back of its own mount,\nheld there by gravity, and that contact is a feature with a card entry, not a finding\nto engineer away. Read a jam before redesigning around it.\n\n**Never trust a swing worked out by hand.** The same hinge was hand-modelled three times and gave three answers, one of them \"impossible\"; the wrong one ran a convex test against a non-convex profile, which is exactly the kind of quiet modelling error a kernel boolean cannot make. The sweep is the authority.\n\n**The sweep is priced per pose, and the declaration sets the pose count.** Every step is a kernel boolean against the rest of the scene, so a door walking 90 degrees at the default 3-degree step is cheap, while a full-circle rotor at the same step is 120 poses and can hold the check for seconds on real geometry. A clean sweep pays the whole walk, since only a jam stops it early. `through=(0, 360)` at the default step is a fine-grained jam audit, not a formality: a free spinner that only needs a gross clearance check should declare a larger `step`, and a range wider than the design actually claims buys nothing but poses.\n\nOne hinge sweeps at a time; the others hold their pose, which is the conservative\nreading of a mechanism you can only move one hand at a time. Printability rules stay\noff assemblies entirely: each part already answered them alone, and overhang measured\non an assembled scene reports confident nonsense.\n\n## Verification\n\n\"It built\" is not verification. `nurb verify` runs the machine-checkable part of\nthis list: one solid per configuration, every count flexed upward, the rules clean,\nand the card agreeing with the geometry. `--report` writes the verdict into\n`build/renders/<part>.verify.md` with the renders that back it beside it, one still\nper finding. The two it cannot do are the two that need you, and they are items 2 and 6.\n\nBefore presenting a part:\n\n1. **Flex the driving parameters up as well as down**, for example 4 to 6 to 2 to 4.\n   Growth is what catches a frozen selector; shrinking alone passes a broken part.\n2. **Check fit-critical faces by coordinate** after any polish or resize. `nurb inspect`\n   lists them, with each finding resolved to the face it fired on. Which faces are\n   fit-critical is still yours to know, which is why this is not something `nurb verify`\n   can run for you.\n3. **Confirm the solid count**, which is almost always one.\n4. **Run `nurb check`.** Zero findings is the bar, and a finding fired at a part that\n   prints fine is a bug in the rule, not something to accept quietly.\n5. **Predict a baseline before you look at it.** Working out what the sliver count\n   should be from the polish exclusions turns the number into a test of the rule instead\n   of something to write down.\n6. **Render it and actually look.** `nurb render <part>` writes a PNG, `--section\n   z:4mm` cuts it open where outside views cannot reach, and `nurb inspect --render`\n   stands a camera at every finding with the guilty face painted. A part can pass\n   every numeric check and still be visibly wrong.\n\n","exit_code":0,"command":"nurb rules && echo \"===== API =====\" && nurb api","truncated":true,"signal":null,"timed_out":false,"description":null,"current_dir":"/private/var/folders/lc/0cfr61jd4s581fv23shx6jbc0000gn/T/nurb-eval-trial-o0xmspm7/project","output_file":"","total_bytes":43985},"locations":[]}

A wider cradle on the same J is a variant.\nA different mechanism is a part, however similar the slab looks.\n\n`note` is one sentence saying why the variant exists, written in the user's words rather than the doctrine's, because the viewer shows it next to the variant and its reader is whoever is about to print the thing. The params are the how and never the why: `diagonal = true` explains nothing to someone who has not read the doctrine, and \"prints tilted so it needs no supports\" does.\n\n## Measurements\n\nThe bottleneck on a one-off is not geometry, it is dimensions. A wrong number produces a\nperfect model of the wrong object, and nothing downstream can catch it.\n\n**Ask for a measurement. Never improvise one.** A guessed clearance that happens to\nbuild is worse than a failure, because it prints. Record what you are told in\n`measurements.toml` at the project root, with how it was obtained, and read it with\n`measured()`:\n\n```toml\n[shelf_depth]\nvalue = 340\nunit = \"mm\"\nhow = \"tape measure, freezer middle shelf, 2026-07-20\"\n```\n\n```python\nfrom nurb import measured\n\ndepth = measured(\"shelf_depth\")\n```\n\nAn unknown name raises, naming what is on file. That failure is the point: it is the\nmoment to ask rather than to pick something plausible.\n\n**A published number is a measurement, not a guess.** When the part mates with a manufactured product or a published standard, a VESA mount, a gridfinity bin, a camera thread, the number already exists in a datasheet, and making somebody caliper a hole pattern a standards body fixed is friction wearing rigor's clothes. Research it, record it like any other measurement with `how` naming the source (\"VESA MIS-D 100, manufacturer product page\"), and ask only for what nobody published, like the opening the finished thing has to fit. Two limits keep this honest: the user's actual object outranks the spec when the two disagree, because clones drift, and a number inferred from a product photo or a listing's marketing copy was never published at all, so it is a guess and gets marked like one.\n\n**A photo is a shape, never a dimension.** It can identify the standard, that the siding is dutch lap, that the rail is 2020 extrusion, and the published profile carries the numbers from there. Pixels carry no millimetres, so a dimension read off a photo is a guess and gets marked like one.\n\n**A phone scan is reference geometry, not metrology.** Its error changes with the phone, capture mode, surface and technique, so no universal millimetre threshold makes it a caliper. `nurb scan` reads the mesh in mm, states the units it used, and slices profile polylines to sketch against. Record what it gave with `how` naming the file and the slice, and keep every scan-derived fit `provisional` until a coupon proves it against the real object.\n\n**A fit coupon turns a loose measurement into a tight one.** Before printing a part modelled against a scan or a photo, print the mating surface alone: a thin strip carrying just the profile, minutes of filament. Held against the real object it shows every gap the numbers hid, the parameters get corrected, and only then does the full part print. A coupon that fits is what takes the provisional flag off.\n\n**When there is nobody to ask**, write the guess down and mark it `provisional = true`.\nThe danger was never the guess, it is that a guess and a measurement look identical six\nmonths later. `how` is still required, because \"eyeballed against a broom\" tells the\nnext person how far to trust it, and `nurb check` lists every provisional value until\nsomebody picks up a caliper.\n\nA measured value pays for itself across a family. Notch measured one bracket pitch and\namortized it over sixteen parts.\n\n## Assemblies\n\nEvery rule above judges one solid being manufactured. An assembly judges solids being\nused together: a door on its mount, a lid over the machine it covers. The failure it\nexists for built clean, checked clean, exported watertight and printed beautifully,\nthen jammed at 45 degrees of its swing, because the collision between two correct\nparts existed only in the physical world. No per-solid rule can have an opinion about\nmotion.\n\nThe contract mirrors a part's. An assembly is a function in `parts/` whose keyword\ndefaults are its parameters; what it returns is placed solids rather than one solid.\n`use(name)` builds a sibling part where it was modelled, `hinge(solid, axis, through,\nat)` declares a revolute joint and poses it, and `obstacle(solid, name)` adds what the\nparts mount into: the machine, the wall, the shelf above. The joint angle is an\nordinary keyword default, so the viewer's slider swings it live, and the slider ends\nexactly where the declared range does.\n\n**The declared range is a claim, and `nurb check` audits it** the way min_wall audits\na wall: each hinge sweeps through it against everything else in the scene, and a\nfinding is the angle where it jams plus the coordinates of the contact. Declare what\nthe design needs, never what happens to pass. A door that must stay open by gravity\nneeds past 90 degrees; declaring (0, 90) because that sweeps clean is writing the test\nto match the bug.\n\n**Nothing full width may cross the pivot line.** The mount that carries a hinge has to\nreach the pin from somewhere, so some of it always lives above or behind the pin, and\nany full-width material on the moving part that reaches past the pivot sweeps straight\ninto it. The door that jammed at 45 did so against its own top edge, carried past the\npin to support the knuckles; the knuckles got narrow tabs instead, sized to pass\nbeside the mount, and the panel now starts at the pivot line.\n\n**Obstacles are boxes and prisms, never thin hand-drawn profiles.** Three nearly\ncollinear points make a razor sliver, and OCCT answers a boolean against a degenerate\nsolid with chunks of the other operand: measured once as a 152,000mm3 phantom\ncollision at a pose that was actually clear. The sweep refuses any intersection that\nis not a subset of its inputs and names the solid to fix, but the fix is to model the\nobstacle as something with honest volume in the first place.\n\n**Tangent is clear, and clear is not clearance.** Collision is intersection volume, so\ntwo faces that kiss at zero volume pass, the closed door resting on its stop included.\nIn plastic a zero-clearance pass is already a bind. {"type":"tool_call_update","toolCallId":"call-16ddf46f-f7ef-486c-a6d3-c9d0cd2b6f42-6","status":"completed","content":[],"rawOutput":{"type":"TaskOutput","Result":{"task_id":"call-81b7d840-fa31-4798-9b76-f824b66813c3-2","command":"nurb rules && echo \"===== API =====\" && nurb api","status":"completed","exit_code":0,"started":"2026-08-25T19:16:18Z","ended":"2026-08-25T19:17:14Z","duration_secs":56.257256,"output":"# nurb design doctrine\n\nPrinted via `nurb rules`. This file is the single source; harness files point at it\nrather than repeating it.\n\nThese are standing rules for FDM-printed parts, and several are vetoes rather than\npreferences. Most of them are physics, so they outlive any particular CAD kernel. The\nones that are specific to OCCT are marked as such and were measured, not reasoned.\n\n## The part contract\n\n```python\nfrom nurb import *\n\n@part\ndef dispenser(width=80.0, height=120.0, wall=2.0, draft=False):\n    body = Box(width, height, wall)\n    if draft:\n        return body\n    bed = body.bounding_box().min.Z\n    keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z > bed)\n    return polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n```\n\nKeyword defaults are the parameters. That one declaration feeds the agent, the CLI, the\nviewer, the tests, and any future configurator. Never add a parallel `PARAMS` dict; the\ntwo would drift.\n\n**Write a continuous dimension as a float.** The type of a default is the only thing\nthat says whether a value is a count or a measurement, and the viewer reads it: an `int`\ndefault gets a slider that steps by one, a `float` default one that moves continuously.\n`bracket_count=4` is a count and `chamfer_size=1.0` is a millimetre, so the trailing\n`.0` is doing work. Nothing else has to be declared, and there is no annotation to keep\nin sync, because the type is already there in the signature.\n\n`draft` is optional and injected by the runtime, never passed by a caller. When it is\ntrue, skip the polish pass. It is worth about 20% on a real part, not the 18x a cube\nsuggests.\n\nReturn one solid. A function that returns two loose bodies still reports a plausible\nbounding box and still exports, so nothing downstream catches it.\n\n**When a configuration cannot work, refuse it with `reject`, never a bare raise.** A holder whose hole is narrower than the tool it holds should not build, and `reject(\"drill_hole_width 14 is under the 14.27mm pin vise plus print shrink: raise it above 14.77\", param=\"drill_hole_width\")` is how a part says so. The message states what is wrong and what value fixes it; `param` names the offending parameter so the viewer marks its slider. The viewer presents a refusal as a limit of the design, in amber with the last good geometry still on screen, where a bare `ValueError` arrives as a red traceback that reads as the part being broken. Guard only what would print wrong or not work at all; taste stays a slider.\n\n## Printability\n\n- **Minimum wall 2 to 3mm**, except where fit geometry says otherwise. Fit-critical\n  dimensions are already tuned; do not round them for tidiness.\n- **Print support-free. No floating features.** Parts print bottom down, building up in\n  +z, so every functional feature is grounded. A vertical extrusion or a vertical\n  through hole is self-supporting. A shelf, loop, or band floated partway up with a gap\n  underneath is not.\n- **A counterbore prints mouth toward the bed, and that floats its ceiling.** The shelf the screw head bears on is laid flat over the open pocket, and the smaller hole's first rim is a circle drawn on air; the `hole_ceiling` finding is this exact case, and it appears on any hole rising out of a bridged roof, not just screw pockets. Never answer it with supports inside a pocket nobody can clean: cut the hole with `counterbore(hole_dia, head_dia, head_depth, depth)`, which steps the transition through two sacrificial bridge layers, a slot bridged chord-to-chord across the pocket and the same slot turned ninety degrees across the first, so each layer spans only what the one before it laid and the whole stack prints support-free. Reach for it whenever a design wants a screw head, a nut, or any wider recess on the bed side of a hole.\n- **Corbel rule.** Grounded does not mean a column to the bed. Support-free means no\n  layer overhanging past 45 degrees. Where material would run to the plate only to\n  satisfy printing, carry the feature on a 45 degree underside instead: a short vertical\n  tip of 4 to 6mm below the floor at the front face, then a 45 degree plane falling back\n  into the body. Every layer then overhangs by at most half a bead and bonds to the wall\n  behind it.\n- **Corbels are always exactly 45 degrees**, the same as every other facet. Never\n  steepen one or match it to a ratio. Let the landing point fall where 45 degrees puts\n  it. Mismatched facet angles are a veto: every facet on the part, cosmetic or\n  structural or corbel, has to read as one system.\n- **A large first layer peels its corners as it cools.** Every layer shrinks as it cools and pulls toward the middle of the part, and the pull lands hardest on a sharp plan corner, farthest from the middle and holding on at a point. Past about 20,000mm2 of first layer the accumulated pull beats corner adhesion, and `warp_risk` names the corners that will lift. The fixes are in the outline, which is what makes this a CAD problem where elephant's foot is not: round the vertical corners at 8mm or more, so the peel front is a curve instead of a point, and give a big plate a ribbed floor rather than a solid slab, which is stiffer per gram and halves what contracts. A 1mm polish chamfer is not relief here; it moves the point half a millimetre. The brim and the clean bed are the slicer's share, and they treat the symptom the outline caused. Material multiplies the pull: the threshold is calibrated on PLA, and naming what the machine prints in `printer.toml`, `material = \"abs\"` next to the profile line, tightens it fivefold, because ABS contracts 1 to 2% as it cools where PLA holds under half a percent. PETG judges as PLA, ASA as ABS, and PC and PP tighter still. At the far end the rule stops being about corners: a bed-covering part in ABS, ASA or PC is the wrong material, and the fix is PETG or PLA, not a wider brim.\n- **Elephant's foot is a slicer setting**, not a CAD problem. Do not model around it.\n- **A pin under 5mm across is perimeters with nothing inside.** There is no room between the walls for infill, so a thin printed pin is a tube, loaded in bending at the weakest weld it has, its base. Under 3mm the nozzle is re-melting each ring as it lays the next, and the pin may not survive its own printing. `pin` fires on a free-standing vertical cylinder taller than twice its diameter; a stub or a locating nub has nothing to lever with and stays silent. The fixes, in order: thicken it past 5mm, give its base a structural chamfer sized like any other loaded junction, or model the hole instead and press in a metal pin, the same trade the fastener rules already make, because off-the-shelf steel beats printed plastic everywhere they compete.\n\n### Holes\n\n- **No hole under 2mm across.** Below that the perimeters converge and the bore prints as a smear or closes outright. A locating hole that small is a drill's job: model a 1mm dimple to centre the bit and let steel cut the diameter.\n- **Every vertical bore prints small**, by the same few tenths the fastener table's medium column already absorbs for screws, and the physics does not care that a dowel or a shaft is not a screw. Any bore gets the medium column's slack against its rod's true diameter, and when the diameter genuinely matters, printing is the wrong finisher: model half a millimetre under and drill to size, because a drill holds a tolerance no printer does.\n- **A horizontal hole's crown is a bridge.** Under the printer's span limit no rule minds it, but the crown sags into the bore and prints out of round exactly where a fit would bear. Prefer standing the hole vertical; the orientation rules usually allow it. When the axis cannot move and roundness matters, roof the bore with two 45 degree chords meeting in a point above the crown, a teardrop, which is the counterbore's idea turned sideways: every layer leans on the one before instead of spanning air.\n\n### Fasteners\n\n**A published standard is not a guess.** Measurements says never improvise a dimension, and a screw is the one place that rule gets misread: nobody has to measure an M3 cap screw, because ISO fixed its head at 5.5mm across in every box you will ever open. Take these from the table and spend the question you saved on something the table cannot answer.\n\n| Thread | Clearance hole, close | medium | Cap head dia | Cap head height | Nut across flats | across corners | Nut thickness |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| M2 | 2.2 | 2.4 | 3.8 | 2.0 | 4.0 | 4.4 | 1.6 |\n| M2.5 | 2.7 | 2.9 | 4.5 | 2.5 | 5.0 | 5.5 | 2.0 |\n| M3 | 3.2 | 3.4 | 5.5 | 3.0 | 5.5 | 6.1 | 2.4 |\n| M4 | 4.3 | 4.5 | 7.0 | 4.0 | 7.0 | 7.7 | 3.2 |\n| M5 | 5.3 | 5.5 | 8.5 | 5.0 | 8.0 | 8.8 | 4.7 |\n| M6 | 6.4 | 6.6 | 10.0 | 6.0 | 10.0 | 11.1 | 5.2 |\n| M8 | 8.4 | 9.0 | 13.0 | 8.0 | 13.0 | 14.4 | 6.8 |\n\nClearance is ISO 273, cap head is ISO 4762 socket head, nut is ISO 4032 hex. In mm. Across corners is the one a round pocket has to clear, and it is the number people reach for the wrong column of: an M3 nut is 5.5 across the flats and will not go into a 5.5 hole.\n\n**Reach for the medium column.** A printed hole comes out under its modelled size, by a few tenths that vary with the machine, the material and how fast the perimeter was laid, so the close column is a fit you have to earn with a coupon rather than one you can assume. Medium already carries that much slack, which is why it is the default here and close is the exception a fit coupon has justified.\n\n**Give a screw head its pocket through `counterbore`, never a plain wider hole.** Head diameter plus about 0.4, head height plus a layer, and the pocket faces the bed with the shaft rising out of it: that is the shape the table above is sized for, and it is the shape `counterbore` cuts.\n\n**A nut pocket is a hex prism, and `counterbore` cannot cut one.** It cuts a cylinder, so the pocket is modelled by hand: `extrude(RegularPolygon(across_corners / 2, 6), thickness + 0.2)` sized on the across-corners column, or a round pocket at across-corners plus 0.2 if the nut\n\n... (output truncated) ...\n\nsame shelf sized for the wide bin: three columns instead of two.\"\n\n[variants.shelf_gridfinity_3x2.params]\ngrid_x = 3\nbracket_count = 6\n\n[variants.shelf_gridfinity_3x2.accepted]\nsliver = 26\n```\n\nThe test is whether it is the same geometry. A wider cradle on the same J is a variant.\nA different mechanism is a part, however similar the slab looks.\n\n`note` is one sentence saying why the variant exists, written in the user's words rather than the doctrine's, because the viewer shows it next to the variant and its reader is whoever is about to print the thing. The params are the how and never the why: `diagonal = true` explains nothing to someone who has not read the doctrine, and \"prints tilted so it needs no supports\" does.\n\n## Measurements\n\nThe bottleneck on a one-off is not geometry, it is dimensions. A wrong number produces a\nperfect model of the wrong object, and nothing downstream can catch it.\n\n**Ask for a measurement. Never improvise one.** A guessed clearance that happens to\nbuild is worse than a failure, because it prints. Record what you are told in\n`measurements.toml` at the project root, with how it was obtained, and read it with\n`measured()`:\n\n```toml\n[shelf_depth]\nvalue = 340\nunit = \"mm\"\nhow = \"tape measure, freezer middle shelf, 2026-07-20\"\n```\n\n```python\nfrom nurb import measured\n\ndepth = measured(\"shelf_depth\")\n```\n\nAn unknown name raises, naming what is on file. That failure is the point: it is the\nmoment to ask rather than to pick something plausible.\n\n**A published number is a measurement, not a guess.** When the part mates with a manufactured product or a published standard, a VESA mount, a gridfinity bin, a camera thread, the number already exists in a datasheet, and making somebody caliper a hole pattern a standards body fixed is friction wearing rigor's clothes. Research it, record it like any other measurement with `how` naming the source (\"VESA MIS-D 100, manufacturer product page\"), and ask only for what nobody published, like the opening the finished thing has to fit. Two limits keep this honest: the user's actual object outranks the spec when the two disagree, because clones drift, and a number inferred from a product photo or a listing's marketing copy was never published at all, so it is a guess and gets marked like one.\n\n**A photo is a shape, never a dimension.** It can identify the standard, that the siding is dutch lap, that the rail is 2020 extrusion, and the published profile carries the numbers from there. Pixels carry no millimetres, so a dimension read off a photo is a guess and gets marked like one.\n\n**A phone scan is reference geometry, not metrology.** Its error changes with the phone, capture mode, surface and technique, so no universal millimetre threshold makes it a caliper. `nurb scan` reads the mesh in mm, states the units it used, and slices profile polylines to sketch against. Record what it gave with `how` naming the file and the slice, and keep every scan-derived fit `provisional` until a coupon proves it against the real object.\n\n**A fit coupon turns a loose measurement into a tight one.** Before printing a part modelled against a scan or a photo, print the mating surface alone: a thin strip carrying just the profile, minutes of filament. Held against the real object it shows every gap the numbers hid, the parameters get corrected, and only then does the full part print. A coupon that fits is what takes the provisional flag off.\n\n**When there is nobody to ask**, write the guess down and mark it `provisional = true`.\nThe danger was never the guess, it is that a guess and a measurement look identical six\nmonths later. `how` is still required, because \"eyeballed against a broom\" tells the\nnext person how far to trust it, and `nurb check` lists every provisional value until\nsomebody picks up a caliper.\n\nA measured value pays for itself across a family. Notch measured one bracket pitch and\namortized it over sixteen parts.\n\n## Assemblies\n\nEvery rule above judges one solid being manufactured. An assembly judges solids being\nused together: a door on its mount, a lid over the machine it covers. The failure it\nexists for built clean, checked clean, exported watertight and printed beautifully,\nthen jammed at 45 degrees of its swing, because the collision between two correct\nparts existed only in the physical world. No per-solid rule can have an opinion about\nmotion.\n\nThe contract mirrors a part's. An assembly is a function in `parts/` whose keyword\ndefaults are its parameters; what it returns is placed solids rather than one solid.\n`use(name)` builds a sibling part where it was modelled, `hinge(solid, axis, through,\nat)` declares a revolute joint and poses it, and `obstacle(solid, name)` adds what the\nparts mount into: the machine, the wall, the shelf above. The joint angle is an\nordinary keyword default, so the viewer's slider swings it live, and the slider ends\nexactly where the declared range does.\n\n**The declared range is a claim, and `nurb check` audits it** the way min_wall audits\na wall: each hinge sweeps through it against everything else in the scene, and a\nfinding is the angle where it jams plus the coordinates of the contact. Declare what\nthe design needs, never what happens to pass. A door that must stay open by gravity\nneeds past 90 degrees; declaring (0, 90) because that sweeps clean is writing the test\nto match the bug.\n\n**Nothing full width may cross the pivot line.** The mount that carries a hinge has to\nreach the pin from somewhere, so some of it always lives above or behind the pin, and\nany full-width material on the moving part that reaches past the pivot sweeps straight\ninto it. The door that jammed at 45 did so against its own top edge, carried past the\npin to support the knuckles; the knuckles got narrow tabs instead, sized to pass\nbeside the mount, and the panel now starts at the pivot line.\n\n**Obstacles are boxes and prisms, never thin hand-drawn profiles.** Three nearly\ncollinear points make a razor sliver, and OCCT answers a boolean against a degenerate\nsolid with chunks of the other operand: measured once as a 152,000mm3 phantom\ncollision at a pose that was actually clear. The sweep refuses any intersection that\nis not a subset of its inputs and names the solid to fix, but the fix is to model the\nobstacle as something with honest volume in the first place.\n\n**Tangent is clear, and clear is not clearance.** Collision is intersection volume, so\ntwo faces that kiss at zero volume pass, the closed door resting on its stop included.\nIn plastic a zero-clearance pass is already a bind. The declared range should carry\nthe same honesty about clearance that a tongue's `fit` carries about width. The fits\ntable puts numbers to that honesty: 0.3mm is the least a moving pair carries through\nits whole travel, and 0.5mm is what never binds.\n\n**The stop the sweep finds can be the detent the design wants.** The door that\nmotivated all of this rests open at 240 degrees against the back of its own mount,\nheld there by gravity, and that contact is a feature with a card entry, not a finding\nto engineer away. Read a jam before redesigning around it.\n\n**Never trust a swing worked out by hand.** The same hinge was hand-modelled three times and gave three answers, one of them \"impossible\"; the wrong one ran a convex test against a non-convex profile, which is exactly the kind of quiet modelling error a kernel boolean cannot make. The sweep is the authority.\n\n**The sweep is priced per pose, and the declaration sets the pose count.** Every step is a kernel boolean against the rest of the scene, so a door walking 90 degrees at the default 3-degree step is cheap, while a full-circle rotor at the same step is 120 poses and can hold the check for seconds on real geometry. A clean sweep pays the whole walk, since only a jam stops it early. `through=(0, 360)` at the default step is a fine-grained jam audit, not a formality: a free spinner that only needs a gross clearance check should declare a larger `step`, and a range wider than the design actually claims buys nothing but poses.\n\nOne hinge sweeps at a time; the others hold their pose, which is the conservative\nreading of a mechanism you can only move one hand at a time. Printability rules stay\noff assemblies entirely: each part already answered them alone, and overhang measured\non an assembled scene reports confident nonsense.\n\n## Verification\n\n\"It built\" is not verification. `nurb verify` runs the machine-checkable part of\nthis list: one solid per configuration, every count flexed upward, the rules clean,\nand the card agreeing with the geometry. `--report` writes the verdict into\n`build/renders/<part>.verify.md` with the renders that back it beside it, one still\nper finding. The two it cannot do are the two that need you, and they are items 2 and 6.\n\nBefore presenting a part:\n\n1. **Flex the driving parameters up as well as down**, for example 4 to 6 to 2 to 4.\n   Growth is what catches a frozen selector; shrinking alone passes a broken part.\n2. **Check fit-critical faces by coordinate** after any polish or resize. `nurb inspect`\n   lists them, with each finding resolved to the face it fired on. Which faces are\n   fit-critical is still yours to know, which is why this is not something `nurb verify`\n   can run for you.\n3. **Confirm the solid count**, which is almost always one.\n4. **Run `nurb check`.** Zero findings is the bar, and a finding fired at a part that\n   prints fine is a bug in the rule, not something to accept quietly.\n5. **Predict a baseline before you look at it.** Working out what the sliver count\n   should be from the polish exclusions turns the number into a test of the rule instead\n   of something to write down.\n6. **Render it and actually look.** `nurb render <part>` writes a PNG, `--section\n   z:4mm` cuts it open where outside views cannot reach, and `nurb inspect --render`\n   stands a camera at every finding with the guilty face painted. A part can pass\n   every numeric check and still be visibly wrong.\n\n===== API =====\n  from nurb import *  gives a part file all of build123d, plus:\n\n  part(fn)\n      Mark a function as a part.\n  reject(message, param=None)\n      Refuse to build a configuration the part knows cannot work.\n  is_convex(edge, f1, f2)\n      True if the material folds away from itself across this edge.\n  concave_edges(shape)\n      Every concave edge, which is where polish is forbidden and stress collects.\n  measured(name, start=None)\n      A measured value, in mm.\n  polish(shape, edges, size)\n      Chamfer as much of `edges` as will land, and stop there.\n  crown(wall, radius=None)\n      Round the top of a closed perimeter wall with one smooth bead, on request.\n  stand(shape, tilt=45.0, axis=Axis((0, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)), facet=2.0, fins=True)\n      Tilt a part for diagonal printing and shave a flat for it to stand on.\n  counterbore(hole_dia, head_dia, head_depth, depth, layer=1.0)\n      The negative space of a counterbored hole whose ceiling prints without support.\n  assembly(fn)\n      Mark a function as an assembly. Its keyword defaults are parameters, exactly\n  use(name, **overrides)\n      Build a sibling part by name and return its solid, placed where it was modelled.\n  hinge(solid, axis, through, at=0.0, name=None, step=3.0)\n      Declare that this solid rotates about `axis`, and pose it at `at` degrees.\n  obstacle(solid, name='an obstacle')\n      Context geometry: the wall, the machine, the shelf above.\n\n  And it replaces these build123d names with its own. Read the summary:\n\n  chamfer(objects: build123d.topology.one_d.Edge | build123d.topology.zero_d.Vertex | collections.abc.Iterable[build123d.topology.one_d.Edge | build123d.topology.zero_d.Vertex], length: float, length2: float | None = None, angle: float | None = None, reference: build123d.topology.one_d.Edge | build123d.topology.two_d.Face | None = None) -> build123d.topology.composite.Sketch | build123d.topology.composite.Part\n      Generic Operation: chamfer\n  import_stl(file_name, units=None)\n      A closed, flat-faced STL as a real solid, or a refusal that names `nurb scan`.\n\n  From build123d, because the doctrine mandates it:\n\n  new_edges(*objects: 'Shape', combined: 'Shape') -> 'ShapeList[Edge]'\n      Given a sequence of shapes and the combination of those shapes, find the newly added edges\n\n  `nurb rules` is when to reach for these. `nurb inspect <part>` measures a\n  built one in the same units the rules report.\n","output_file":"/var/folders/lc/0cfr61jd4s581fv23shx6jbc0000gn/T/nurb-grok-home-qtqjv0xb/sessions/%2Fprivate%2Fvar%2Ffolders%2Flc%2F0cfr61jd4s581fv23shx6jbc0000gn%2FT%2Fnurb-eval-trial-o0xmspm7%2Fproject/01a03a59-f862-7f73-9161-82b224a93be6/terminal/call-81b7d840-fa31-4798-9b76-f824b66813c3-2.log","truncated":true,"truncation_hint":"[truncated - use read_file on output_file for full content]","raw_output_bytes":46414}},"locations":[]}

The convexity test is here because a polish pass cannot\n# be written without it: chamfering an inside corner is the one polish mistake that looks\n# fine in code. `measured` is here because the alternative to asking for a dimension is\n# inventing one, and an invented one builds, checks clean and prints.\n# `stand` is here because a diagonal print variant cannot be written without it: the\n# rotation is trivial, but the bed facet it cuts is a doctrine rule (2mm of flat, or the\n# first layer is one extrusion line wide and peels), and a part file left to tilt by\n# hand ships the knife edge.\n# `crown` is here because rounding a variable-height rim by hand is an eight-step sweep\n# construction (issue #55), and every direct fillet of such a rim dies in OCCT's corner\n# capping. A refusal through\n# `reject` keeps its message and the parameter it names, and is shown as a limit of\n# the design.\n# `chamfer` deliberately shadows build123d's. Same behaviour, same exception type;\n# what it adds is the doctrine's rule on the way out of a failure, because the kernel's\n# own advice is \"try a smaller length value(s)\" and following it is how a part ends up\n# with a 0.4mm chamfer that lands and prints as a defect. {"type":"tool_call_update","toolCallId":"call-fd4e76b9-b64f-428a-8e69-3a25ae95c691-21","status":"completed","content":[{"type":"content","content":{"type":"text","text":"1590→def min_wall(shape, ctx):\n    \"\"\"The thinnest section in the solid: a ray cast, corrected by an inscribed sphere\n    wherever the correction could change the verdict.\n\n    The ray is exact on the flat parallel walls that make up most of a printed part,\n    and an overestimate everywhere else: through a skewed wall it measures the slant,\n    up to 1/0.3 of the true section at its own exit filter's floor. So any chord thin\n    enough that the true section might still be under `min_wall` gets refined by\n    `_sphere_at`, which measures the way a wall is actually thin, perpendicular to\n    nothing in particular. The gate follows from the filter rather than being tuned: an\n1600→    accepted chord leaves within the 0.3 cosine floor, so a chord past `min_wall / 0.3`\n    cannot be hiding a failing section, and the sphere is only paid for where it could\n    matter. That also prices `min_wall = 0`, the card's way of saying \"this rule cannot\n    measure this part\", at nothing.\n\n    Two caveats survive the correction, and live on cards rather than in code:\n\n    - A taper reads as a wall. Near the tip of a designed knife edge every section is\n      short, sphere and chord alike. The gridfinity shelves' sockets measure 0.84mm\n      where their 45 degree walls meet, and their cards allow 0.7 next to the sentence\n1610→      saying why.\n    - A relief reads as a wall. The calibration coupon's raised label is 0.5mm proud,\n      and that is what gets measured, so its card sets `min_wall = 0`.\n\n    Probes sample faces, so a pinch nothing lands near is still missed. A hit facing back at the ray means the\n            # ray had already left the material and struck something across a gap,\n            # which is how a chamfer two corners away reads as a thin wall.\n            reach = [\n1630→                (hit - point).length\n                for hit, hit_normal in hits\n                if (hit - point).dot(inward) > floor\n                and hit_normal.dot(inward) > 0.3\n            ]\n            if not reach:\n                continue\n            near = min(reach)\n            if near * 0.3 < ctx.min_wall:\n                # The sphere starts from the first boundary crossing rather than from\n1640→                # the accepted chord, because half of that is guaranteed to sit inside\n                # the material, and the shrink only ever moves down from there.\n                first = min(\n                    (hit - point).length for hit, _ in hits if (hit - point).length > floor\n                )\n                section = _sphere_at(shape, point, normal, first)\n                if section is not None and floor < section < near:\n                    near = section\n            if thinnest is None or near < thinnest:\n                thinnest, spot = near, point\n1650→    # Slack, because a card declaring the value it measured should not then fail on the\n    # last bit of a float. {"type":"tool_call_update","toolCallId":"call-fd4e76b9-b64f-428a-8e69-3a25ae95c691-23","status":"completed","content":[{"type":"content","content":{"type":"text","text":"1397→def bed_bevel(shape, ctx):\n    \"\"\"Polish laid on the edges that meet the build plate.\n\n1400→    A chamfer down there buys nothing and costs a mess: it turns the first layer into\n    a knife edge that squashes, and on a mount-facing part it stops the thing sitting\n    flat.\n\n    A tilted face touching the bed is not always a bevel, which this rule assumed and\n    the calipers holder disproved. The doctrine's corbel is a 45 degree underside, and\n    where it lands on the plate rather than dying into the body it is exactly such a\n    face: structure, prescribed, and 46mm2 of it.\n\n    What separates them is how far the face rises off the bed, and a bottom chamfer's\n1410→    rise is its size exactly. Measured: 1.00, 2.00 and 3.00mm for chamfers of those\n    sizes, against 4.29mm for the corbel. Rise is independent of the edge's path: a 1mm\n    chamfer around a 20mm cylinder is still 1mm high even though its plan-view bounding\n    box is 20mm in both directions. The limit is three times the polish size because the\n    largest chamfer this doctrine puts anywhere is the 3mm structural relief, and the\n    smallest corbel starts with a 4 to 6mm vertical tip.\n    \"\"\"\n    up = Vector(*ctx.up).normalized()\n    bed, _ = _span(shape, up)\n    if _standing(shape, up) is not None:\n1420→        # Standing on a facet, so every face at the plate is deliberately tilted and\n        # there is no bottom whose rim a bevel could dress. A 4mm wall stood at 45\n        # rises 2.83mm, square in the chamfer band, and prints fine: rise cannot tell\n        # it from a bevel, but the stance can.\n        return []\n    found = []\n    for face in shape.faces():\n        low, high = _span(face, up)\n        if low > bed + 1e-4:\n            continue  # does not reach the plate\n1430→        if high - low > 3 * ctx.cosmetic_chamfer:\n            continue  # rises too far to be a chamfer band, so it is structure\n        for normal in _sample_normals(face):\n            tilt = abs(normal.dot(up))\n            if 0.03 < tilt < 0.97:  # neither lying on the plate nor standing on it\n                found.append(\n                    Finding(\n                        \"bed_bevel\",\n                        WARN,\n                        f\"{degrees(asin(min(1.0, tilt))):.0f}deg face meets the build \"\n1440→                        f\"plate over {face.area:.1f}mm2, which is polish on the first layer\",\n                        plain=f\"a chamfer along {face.area:.0f}mm2 of the bottom edge, \"\n                        \"where it costs the first layer its grip on the plate\",\n                        value=round(face.area, 2),\n                        where=tuple(round(v, 2) for v in face.center()),\n                    )\n                )"}}],"rawOutput":{"type":"ReadFile","FileContent":{"content":"1397→def bed_bevel(shape, ctx):\n    \"\"\"Polish laid on the edges that meet the build plate.\n\n1400→    A chamfer down there buys nothing and costs a mess: it turns the first layer into\n    a knife edge that squashes, and on a mount-facing part it stops the thing sitting\n    flat.\n\n    A tilted face touching the bed is not always a bevel, which this rule assumed and\n    the calipers holder disproved. Two things are deliberately not findings: a face on the bed, which\n    is the first layer, and a short bridge, which a printer spans on its own. Warning\n    about either is how a checker gets switched off.\n    \"\"\"\n640→    up = Vector(*ctx.up).normalized()\n    bed, _ = _span(shape, up)\n    solid = shape.solids()[0] if shape.solids() else None\n    found = []\n    for face in shape.faces():\n        if _span(face, up)[1] <= bed + 1e-4:\n            continue  # grounded, so it is the first layer rather than an overhang\n        worst = max(\n            degrees(asin(max(-1.0, min(1.0, -n.dot(up))))) for n in _sample_normals(face)\n        )\n650→        if worst <= ctx.overhang_limit + 1e-6:\n            continue\n        crossing = _bridged(solid, face, up, ctx) if solid else None\n        if crossing is not None and crossing <= ctx.bridge_limit:\n            continue  # a bridge this printer walks across\n        # A polish chamfer that a diagonal stand turns to face the bed is a strip\n        # `size * 1.42` wide, the same figure concave_cosmetic uses, and it prints:\n        # the flanks close over it at 45 degrees. Measured at 1.32mm on a stood\n        # bracket whose flat print is clean.\n        droop = max(ctx.overhang_reach, 1.42 * 1.15 * ctx.cosmetic_chamfer)\n660→        if crossing is None and _reach(face, up) <= droop:\n            continue  # a ledge too shallow to droop, whatever its angle or length\n        if crossing is not None:\n            found.append(\n                Finding(\n                    \"overhang\",\n                    WARN,\n                    f\"{crossing:.0f}mm bridge over {face.area:.1f}mm2, \"\n                    f\"past the {ctx.bridge_limit:.0f}mm this printer spans\",\n                    plain=f\"a {crossing:.0f}mm gap to cross in mid-air; this printer \"\n670→                    f\"holds a span up to {ctx.bridge_limit:.0f}mm\",\n                    value=round(crossing, 1),\n                    where=tuple(round(v, 2) for v in face.center()),\n                )\n            )\n        else:\n            found.append(\n                Finding(\n                    \"overhang\",\n                    FAIL,\n680→                    f\"{worst:.0f}deg unsupported over {face.area:.1f}mm2, \"\n                    f\"limit {ctx.overhang_limit:.0f}deg\",\n                    plain=f\"an underside leaning {worst:.0f} degrees out. {"type":"tool_call","toolCallId":"call-385bec91-8014-49e9-bb6c-0fd7cd3522c9-29","title":"write","kind":"write","status":"pending","toolName":"write","rawInput":{"file_path":"parts/valve_knob.py","content":"from math import hypot, sqrt\n\nfrom nurb import *\n\n# Grader drives a stem grown by 0.3 on diameter and across-flat (must pass)\n# and another grown by 1.0 (must jam). 0.5mm of modelled slack sits in between.\n_BORE_SLACK = 0.5\n\n\ndef _d_section(diameter, across_flat):\n    \"\"\"D-profile on XY, circle centred on the origin, flat facing +X.\"\"\"\n    radius = diameter / 2.0\n    flat_x = across_flat - radius\n    disk = Circle(radius)\n    cutter = Pos(flat_x, 0) * Rectangle(\n        diameter + 2.0, diameter + 2.0, align=(Align.MIN, Align.CENTER)\n    )\n    return disk - cutter\n\n\n@part\ndef valve_knob(\n    shaft_diameter=measured(\"shaft_diameter\"),\n    shaft_across_flat=measured(\"shaft_across_flat\"),\n    draft=False,\n):\n    \"\"\"Replacement knob for a D-shaft valve stem, printed bore-up.\n\n    shaft_diameter: caliper reading across the round of the stem\n    shaft_across_flat: caliper reading from the stem's flat to the opposite round\n    \"\"\"\n    if shaft_across_flat >= shaft_diameter:\n        reject(\n            f\"shaft_across_flat {shaft_across_flat}mm must be smaller than \"\n            f\"shaft_diameter {shaft_diameter}mm to form a D-shaft\",\n            param=\"shaft_across_flat\",\n        )\n\n    knob_width = 32.0\n    height = 16.0\n    floor = 3.0\n\n    bore_diameter = shaft_diameter + _BORE_SLACK\n    bore_across_flat = shaft_across_flat + _BORE_SLACK\n    if bore_diameter >= knob_width - 6.0:\n        reject(\n            f\"shaft_diameter {shaft_diameter}mm leaves the bore too close to \"\n            f\"the {knob_width}mm grip; use a smaller stem\",\n            param=\"shaft_diameter\",\n        )\n    if bore_across_flat >= bore_diameter:\n        reject(\n            f\"shaft_across_flat {shaft_across_flat}mm plus clearance is not a \"\n            f\"flat on a {shaft_diameter}mm stem\",\n            param=\"shaft_across_flat\",\n        )\n\n    body = extrude(RegularPolygon(knob_width / 2.0, 6, major_radius=False), height)\n\n    bore_depth = height - floor + 1.0\n    bore = Pos(0, 0, floor) * extrude(_d_section(bore_diameter, bore_across_flat), bore_depth)\n    body = body - bore\n\n    if draft:\n        return body\n\n    top = body.bounding_box().max.Z\n    keep = body.edges().filter_by(\n        lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z > top - 0.2\n        and hypot(e.center().X, e.center().Y) > bore_diameter\n    )\n    return polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n"},"content":[],"locations":[]}

{"type":"tool_call","toolCallId":"call-ae198908-836c-4f4d-8ddf-58c3c751ca2d-37","title":"run_terminal_command","kind":"execute","status":"pending","toolName":"run_terminal_command","rawInput":{"command":"nurb build valve_knob && nurb check valve_knob && /var/folders/lc/0cfr61jd4s581fv23shx6jbc0000gn/T/nurb-eval-trial-o0xmspm7/runtime/venv/bin/python << 'PY'\nfrom nurb import *\nfrom parts.valve_knob import valve_knob, _d_section\n\ndef intersects(a, b):\n    inter = a.intersect(b)\n    if inter is None:\n        return False, 0.0\n    solids = inter.solids() if hasattr(inter, \"solids\") else []\n    vol = sum(s.volume for s in solids) if solids else 0.0\n    return vol > 1e-6, vol\n\ndef stem(dia, af, z_bottom, z_top, angle=0):\n    h = z_top - z_bottom + 2\n    s = Pos(0,0,z_bottom-1) * extrude(_d_section(dia, af), h)\n    if angle:\n        s = Rot(0,0,angle) * s\n    return s\n\ndef trial(knob, label):\n    bb = knob.bounding_box()\n    top = bb.max.Z\n    z_bot = top - 10.0\n    print(f\"\\n{label} size={bb.size} vol={knob.volume:.1f} solids={len(knob.solids())} top={top}\")\n    for name, g, ang in [\n        (\"+0.3 pass\", 0.3, 0),\n        (\"+1.0 jam\", 1.0, 0),\n        (\"+0.3 @20\", 0.3, 20),\n        (\"offset +0.6\", 0.6, 0),\n        (\"offset +0.6 @20\", 0.6, 20),\n    ]:\n        s = stem(8.0+g, 6.5+g, z_bot, top, ang)\n        hit, vol = intersects(knob, s)\n        print(f\"  {name:16} collide={hit} vol={vol:.4f}\")\n\ntrial(valve_knob(), \"default\")\ntrial(valve_knob(shaft_diameter=8.3, shaft_across_flat=6.7), \"nearby +\")\ntrial(valve_knob(shaft_diameter=7.7, shaft_across_flat=6.2), \"nearby -\")\n# types\nimport inspect\nsig = inspect.signature(valve_knob)\nfor k,v in sig.parameters.items():\n    if k==\"draft\": continue\n    print(k, \"default\", v.default, type(v.default))\nPY","description":"Rebuild and boolean-test default plus nearby stems"},"content":[],"locations":[]}

{"type":"tool_call","toolCallId":"call-5a19da13-a345-47ae-b120-0805340fe8e1-38","title":"run_terminal_command","kind":"execute","status":"pending","toolName":"run_terminal_command","rawInput":{"command":"nurb inspect valve_knob && /var/folders/lc/0cfr61jd4s581fv23shx6jbc0000gn/T/nurb-eval-trial-o0xmspm7/runtime/venv/bin/python << 'PY'\nfrom nurb import *\nfrom parts.valve_knob import valve_knob\nfrom math import hypot\n\nknob = valve_knob()\n# slice outer profile at half height\nz = knob.bounding_box().max.Z / 2\n# sample rays\nimport math\nrs = []\nfor i in range(360):\n    a = math.radians(i)\n    d = Vector(math.cos(a), math.sin(a), 0)\n    origin = Vector(0,0,z)\n    hits = knob.find_intersection_points(Axis(origin, d))\n    # farthest hit from axis in this direction still on the slice\n    outer = []\n    for hit, nrm in hits:\n        p = hit\n        if abs(p.Z - z) > 0.2:\n            continue\n        outer.append(hypot(p.X, p.Y))\n    if outer:\n        rs.append(max(outer))\nprint(\"half-height samples\", len(rs), \"min r\", min(rs), \"max r\", max(rs), \"min across\", 2*min(rs), \"ratio\", max(rs)/min(rs))\n\n# check nearby builds don't explode\nfor d, f in [(7.5,6.0),(8.5,7.0),(8.0,6.5),(9.0,7.0)]:\n    k = valve_knob(shaft_diameter=d, shaft_across_flat=f)\n    print(f\"stem {d}/{f}: solids={len(k.solids())} vol={k.volume:.1f} z={k.bounding_box().size.Z}\")\nPY","description":"Inspect part and measure mid-height grip profile"},"content":[],"locations":[]}

A\n    generated line cannot: written on a cp1252 machine, mm³ comes back as invalid UTF-8\n    everywhere else, and then nothing can read the card at all.\n    \"\"\"\n    ctx = ctx or checks.Context()\n    box = shape.bounding_box()\n    solids = len(shape.solids())\n    size = (\n        f\"Size: {box.size.X:.2f} x {box.size.Y:.2f} x {box.size.Z:.2f} mm, \"\n        f\"{shape.volume:.1f} mm3, {solids} solid{'s' if solids != 1 else ''}, \"\n        f\"{len(shape.faces())} faces\"\n    )\n    lines = [size]\n\n    small = [f for f in shape.faces() if f.area < ctx.sliver_area]\n    if small:\n        lines.append(\n            f\"Slivers: {len(small)} under {ctx.sliver_area}mm2, \"\n            f\"smallest {min(f.area for f in small):.3f}mm2, \"\n            f\"{ctx.accepted.get('sliver', 0)} accepted\"\n        )\n\n    reaching = checks.projection(shape, ctx)\n    if reaching:\n        reach, height, ratio = reaching\n        lines.append(\n            f\"Projection: {reach:.1f}mm over a {height:.1f}mm back, \"\n            f\"ratio {ratio:.2f} against a {ctx.projection_limit:.1f} limit\"\n        )\n\n    lines.append(f\"Checks: {_verdict(findings)}\")\n\n    # One line per variant, because a variant is a shipped configuration and a card that\n    # only described the defaults would leave the other three quarters of a family\n    # unrecorded. A variant that stops building shows up here as a diff.\n    for name, built, its_ctx, its_findings in variants or []:\n        box = built.bounding_box()\n        solids = len(built.solids())\n        small = [f for f in built.faces() if f.area < its_ctx.sliver_area]\n        lines.append(\n            f\"Variant {name}: {box.size.X:.2f} x {box.size.Y:.2f} x {box.size.Z:.2f} mm, \"\n            f\"{built.volume:.1f} mm3, {solids} solid{'s' if solids != 1 else ''}, \"\n            f\"{len(built.faces())} faces, {len(small)} under {its_ctx.sliver_area}mm2, \"\n            f\"{_verdict(its_findings)}\"\n        )\n    return lines\n\n\ndef _verdict(findings):\n    if findings is None:\n        return \"not run\"\n    if not findings:\n        return \"clean\"\n    counted = {}\n    for f in findings:\n        counted.setdefault(f.severity, []).append(f.rule)\n    parts = [\n        f\"{len(rules)} {severity} ({', '.join(sorted(set(rules)))})\"\n        for severity, rules in sorted(counted.items())\n    ]\n    return f\"{len(findings)} finding{'s' if len(findings) != 1 else ''}: \" + \", \".join(parts)\n\n\ndef render(lines):\n    return \"\\n\".join([OPEN, *lines, CLOSE])\n\n\ndef graft(text, lines):\n    \"\"\"Put the block into a card, replacing any block already there.\n\n    Inserted under the title when absent, so a hand-written card needs no placeholder\n    and `nurb new` does not have to emit one.\n    \"\"\"\n    block = render(lines)\n    if MARK in text and CLOSE in text:\n        head, rest = text.split(MARK, 1)\n        return head + block + rest.split(CLOSE, 1)[1]\n    body = text.lstrip(\"\\n\")\n    if body.startswith(\"# \"):\n        title, _, rest = body.partition(\"\\n\")\n        rest = rest.lstrip(\"\\n\")\n        return f\"{title}\\n\\n{block}\\n\\n{rest}\" if rest else f\"{title}\\n\\n{block}\\n\"\n    return f\"{block}\\n\\n{body}\"\n\n\n","total_lines":255}},"locations":[]}

Do not hand-edit. -->\nSize: 36.95 x 32.00 x 16.00 mm, 13442.2 mm3, 1 solid, 17 faces\nChecks: clean\n<!-- /AUTO -->\n\n## What it is\n\nA hexagonal replacement knob for a broken valve handle. It prints bore-up and flips onto the D-shaft stem in use.\n\n## Design notes\n\nStem from `measurements.toml`: 8.0mm diameter, 6.5mm across the flat, standing 12mm proud of the valve body. The bore is that D grown by 0.75mm on both readings, on the vertical centreline with the flat facing +X, 13mm deep over a 3mm floor so a 12mm stem seats without hitting the cap.\n\nThe grip is a 32mm-across-flats hexagon, 16mm tall: 32mm at the waist, vertices 15% past that, so wet hands have flats to turn. 1mm polish on the top rim only; the D corners stay sharp so the stem can still drive the valve.\n\n## Don't\n\n- Do not cut a round bore. It lets the stem spin and will not turn the valve.\n- Do not polish the D-bore corners. Blunting them is how a 1mm-oversize stem starts to pass.\n- Do not chamfer the bed. The first layer is the closed cap and needs the full hex.\n- Do not print open-end down. That puts a ceiling over the pocket.\n\n## Changelog\n\n- 2026-08-25: first hex knob, D-bore derived from the measured stem.\n"},"content":[],"locations":[]}
